lessons.title: Receiving and checking seed samples
lessons.html:
Receiving and checking seed samples

Every seed test in the laboratory starts with sample reception. If a sample is wrongly labelled, damaged or not representative, every test result that follows is worthless. The receiving clerk or analyst is the gatekeeper of the laboratory.

Where samples come from

  • The company's own processing plant, sampling seed lots for labelling
  • Seed inspectors, for certification
  • Contract growers and other seed companies
  • Farmers or dealers with a complaint
  • Research and breeding programmes

What a sample must arrive with

  • A submission form: sender, contact details, crop, cultivar, lot number, lot size, tests requested (purity, germination, moisture, viability and so on) and any seed treatment.
  • A sample that is sealed and labelled with the same lot number.
  • For moisture tests, a moisture-proof sealed container.

Checking the sample

  1. Check that the label on the sample matches the submission form.
  2. Check that the seal is intact. A broken seal means the sample may have been changed.
  3. Check the sample size is enough for the tests requested, according to the testing rules your laboratory follows (usually ISTA rules).
  4. Look at the condition: wet, mouldy, insect-damaged or torn packaging.
  5. Check if the seed is treated. Treated seed is often coloured; handle it with gloves.

Problems

If a sample does not meet requirements, for example the label does not match, the seal is broken or the sample is too small, do not simply test it. Record the problem and contact the sender, following laboratory procedure. The sender may need to send a new sample, or the laboratory may test it with a note on the report.

lessons.title: Registering and passing on samples
lessons.html:
Registering and passing on samples

Once a sample is accepted, it must be registered so that it can be traced through every step of testing.

Registering

  1. Give the sample a unique laboratory number from the register or laboratory system.
  2. Capture all information from the submission form: sender, crop, cultivar, lot number, tests requested, date and time received.
  3. Write or stick the laboratory number on the sample bag and on the submission form.
  4. Record the condition of the sample on receipt.
  5. Record who received it.

Why a unique number?

Two samples may have the same lot number from different senders, or the same cultivar name. The laboratory number makes each sample unique. From now on, the sample is always identified by this number on every worksheet, tray and envelope.

Passing samples to the analysts

  • Sort samples by test and priority. Urgent samples, for example seed needed for planting soon, may be flagged as the laboratory procedure allows.
  • Pass samples to the right section with the worksheet or test request.
  • Moisture samples go first, before they can gain or lose moisture.
  • Store samples waiting for testing in a cool, dry, secure area.

Confidentiality

Test results and sample information belong to the client. Do not discuss them with other clients or outsiders.

Safety and housekeeping

Wear gloves when handling treated seed. Do not eat or drink in the receiving area. Keep the receiving bench clean so seed from one sample does not get into another. Dispose of packaging properly.

Key points

  • Check that sample label, seal and submission form match.
  • Check the sample size is enough for the tests requested.
  • Record and report problem samples; do not simply test them.
  • Give each sample a unique laboratory number and use it everywhere.
  • Send moisture samples for testing first and store others cool and dry.
